title: The Fallacy of Supply and Demand
coreMove: Build your own estimate before the first visible number turns into the ruler for every later judgment.
sourcePressure: The source emphasizes anchoring, arbitrary coherence, and how initial prices shape later demand even when the first number had little real meaning.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version treats this as negotiation advice; the real move is to notice how the first number installs a private scale.

counterintuition: People know what things should cost

exampleSpecs.audience: a hobby grower attending a regional orchid sale for the first time
exampleSpecs.stakes: letting an opening auction estimate make every later plant seem affordable
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before bidding starts, the grower writes a maximum price based on bloom health and care difficulty, then watches the auctioneer's opening number try to pull it upward
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a greenhouse bench lined with white tags and mist on the glass panes

exampleSpecs.domain: independent bakery buying a used deck oven
exampleSpecs.audience: a bakery owner comparing equipment listings with no prior market knowledge
exampleSpecs.stakes: treating a seller's first inflated listing as the center of the market
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner calls two repair technicians for replacement-part estimates before letting the first listing define the oven's value
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a soot-dark oven listing printed beside a flour-dusted calculator

exampleSpecs.domain: minor-league team setting souvenir cap prices
exampleSpecs.audience: a merch manager deciding the first price fans will see on opening weekend
exampleSpecs.stakes: creating an anchor that shapes what fans call reasonable all season
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager compares two weeks of sales after the first rack displayed the premium cap at eye level before cheaper caps appeared
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a wire cap rack rolling onto the concourse before the gates open

exampleSpecs.audience: a town administrator comparing contractor bids for storm cleanup
exampleSpecs.stakes: mistaking the first emergency bid for the normal cost of tree work
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the administrator writes the cost per block from last year's routine work in the margin before reading the emergency contractor's number aloud
exampleSpecs.firstImage: wet maple limbs stacked beside a council packet after a nor'easter

exampleSpecs.domain: wedding photographer package selection at a venue fair
exampleSpecs.audience: a couple comparing packages after seeing a luxury display first
exampleSpecs.stakes: normalizing an expensive package because the first booth made it look moderate
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: one partner closes the glossy brochure and names the number they would have expected yesterday before they walked into the fair
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a glossy album open under string lights at a venue fair booth

exampleSpecs.domain: used laboratory freezer purchase for a community clinic
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinic operations lead buying equipment with grant money
exampleSpecs.stakes: using the first refurbished freezer quote as the anchor for all later safety judgments
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after seeing the first quote, the lead builds a requirement sheet around temperature logs and service history, then rechecks whether the quote still looks fair
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a temperature log binder lying beside a dented freezer photo

skillTargets: identify the anchor before comparing later numbers
explain arbitrary coherence in a new pricing scene
evaluate whether a later bargain is only distance from a bad first number

tryThisNowSpec: Before opening the next quote, listing, or menu, write the number you would consider fair and the reason for it; then compare the visible price to that note, not to the seller's first anchor.
